title: Is Arthritis Hereditary?

content:
Arthritis can run in families, but it is rarely passed on directly from parent to child. Genes can raise your risk of several types, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and gout. Having a relative with arthritis does not mean you will get it, and lifestyle factors such as weight, smoking and joint injury also play a big part.

How genes affect risk

Most types of arthritis are caused by a mix of many genes, each having a small effect, plus environmental factors. This is different from conditions caused by a single faulty gene, where the chance of passing it on can be calculated precisely. For arthritis, a family history raises the chance but does not determine the outcome.

Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis tends to run in families, particularly in the hands, hips and knees. Knobbly finger joints often appear in several women in the same family. Other factors are also important, such as age, being overweight, previous joint injuries, joint shape and occupation. These can be more influential than genes.

Rheumatoid arthritis

Having a parent or sibling with RA raises your risk, but most people with a family history do not develop it. Several genes are involved, especially those that control the immune system. Smoking is the strongest environmental trigger, particularly in people with certain genes. Not smoking is one of the most useful things relatives of people with RA can do.

Psoriatic arthritis

Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis often run in families. If a close relative has psoriatic arthritis and you have psoriasis, mention it to your GP, especially if you notice joint pain, swollen fingers or toes or nail changes.

Ankylosing spondylitis

Many people with AS carry a gene called HLA-B27. However, most people with HLA-B27 never develop AS, so testing healthy relatives is not usually helpful. If you have a relative with AS and develop long-lasting back pain that is worse with rest and better with movement, tell your GP.

Gout

Gout can run in families because genes affect how the kidneys clear uric acid. Diet, alcohol, weight, kidney function and some medicines also play a part.

Lupus and juvenile arthritis

Lupus and other autoimmune diseases are more common in families with autoimmune conditions, though the risk to each relative remains low. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis rarely affects more than one child in a family.

Should I have a genetic test?

Genetic tests are not routinely used to predict arthritis risk. Some tests, such as HLA-B27, may help doctors with diagnosis when someone already has symptoms. Home genetic testing kits cannot tell you whether you will develop arthritis, and results can be confusing. Speak to your GP if you are worried.

What you can do if arthritis runs in your family

  • keep to a healthy weight
  • stay active and keep your muscles strong
  • protect your joints from injury and complete rehabilitation after sports injuries
  • do not smoke
  • keep alcohol within recommended limits
  • get symptoms checked early, especially joint swelling, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes or pain in several joints

Talking to your children

If you have arthritis, it is natural to worry about your children. You can reassure them that most children of people with arthritis do not develop the same condition, and that if they do, it can be treated. Share healthy habits as a family and encourage them to tell a doctor about joint symptoms. If you are planning a pregnancy and take medicines for arthritis, talk to your rheumatology team, as some medicines need to be changed in advance.

Remember that family history is only one piece of the picture. Many people with arthritis have no relatives with the condition, and many with a strong family history stay well.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
